title: How to Choose a Fractional CFO: What to Verify First
summary: How to choose a fractional CFO comes down to what you verify before you commit. See the criteria that matter, the questions to ask, and what scope to agree.
body_markdown:
## How to Choose a Fractional CFO


How to choose a fractional CFO starts with naming the operational complexity your current finance setup can’t handle, then verifying five things before you sign. Those five are depth of real operating experience at comparable complexity, whether the work is forward-looking or reporting dressed up as strategy, who specifically does the work and what happens when that person changes, the cadence and response time you’re actually buying, and how the CFO will coordinate with the people who keep your books. Owners bring this question to indinero holding two or three proposals that all sound qualified, with no way to tell them apart.


Price is the last question, not the first.


That ordering sounds backwards, because nearly every selection guide leads with credentials and rate cards. It’s also why engagements end in a beautifully formatted reporting package and no better decisions. Every candidate sounds qualified when you haven’t written down the question.


So write it down first. One page, in your own words, naming what your current setup can’t answer. Most owners find the page starts with one of these four sentences.


- “We’re profitable on paper and there’s never enough cash.”
- “Growth feels more chaotic, not less.”
- “Margins are slipping and I don’t know why.”
- “We’re sitting on cash with no plan to deploy it.”


Then score your complexity, line by line. Mark each one simple, getting complicated, or already past you.


- **Entity and ownership structure.** One entity or several, intercompany activity, related-party rent, multiple owners with different expectations.
- **Revenue mix.** One line or several at materially different margins, plus contract terms that govern when cash actually arrives.
- **Working capital drag.** Days sales outstanding nobody can quote, inventory turnover, subcontractors, vendor terms you’ve never renegotiated.
- **Footprint and outside obligations.** Multi-state payroll, sales and use tax exposure, bank debt with covenants, a lender expecting a package on a schedule.
- **The decision pipeline.** A lease renewal, a new location, a senior hire, a large contract whose true margin nobody has modeled, a pricing change you keep postponing.


That page is your scoring rubric, and it’s also why the title on a proposal tells you so little. AICPA and CIMA describe the modern finance leader’s job as[the move from reporting data to generating business outcomes](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/professional-insights/article/how-modern-cfos-drive-business-value-creation) . The label moved faster than the practice did, so you have to test for it rather than read it off a resume. For the short version of the role, start with[what a fractional CFO is](https://www.indinero.com/faq/what-is-a-fractional-cfo/) . If you’re still deciding whether you need one at all,[when to hire a CFO](https://www.indinero.com/blog/when-to-hire-a-cfo-stage-guide/) works the timing question by complexity instead of by size.


## What to Evaluate Before You Commit


What to look for in a fractional CFO sorts into five dimensions, and the order you test them in matters. Operating depth at your level of complexity. Forward-looking versus reporting-focused work. Who does the work. Cadence and responsiveness. Coordination with the people who keep your books. Evaluating a fractional CFO on four of the five and hoping on the fifth isn’t a pass. The weak dimension is where the engagement fails.


**1. Operating depth at comparable complexity.** You aren’t testing years of experience or the logos on a resume. You’re testing whether this person has run a finance function through the mechanics you’re living in. Ask for a past situation that matches a line on your complexity page, then listen for mechanism. Someone who has done the work talks about the chart of accounts they rebuilt to see margin by segment, the collections cadence they installed and what days sales outstanding did over the next two quarters, the vendor terms they renegotiated. Someone who hasn’t talks about frameworks and dashboards. Complexity adjacency also beats industry adjacency. A candidate who has handled inventory turns, multi-state payroll, and covenant reporting in another industry usually fits better than a same-industry candidate whose career sat in a single-entity service business with no inventory and no debt.


**2. Forward-looking work, or reporting with a strategic label.** This is the highest-yield test and the one most selection guides skip. Good CFO work splits across two horizons that aren’t interchangeable. Continuous work means rolling forecasts of revenue, expenses, profitability, and cash, updated as conditions move rather than rebuilt once a year. Event-driven work means modeling one discrete decision. Lease versus buy. The true margin on one large contract. Whether a new territory clears its cost of entry. Make the distinction itself an interview test. A real finance leader separates the two in a sentence and names different outputs for each. A candidate who blurs them, or who answers both halves by walking you through a monthly reporting package, is selling reporting with a strategic label on it.


The gap is wide in practice. AFP’s[2026 FP&A Benchmarking Survey](https://www.financialprofessionals.org/about/learn-more/press-releases/Details/afp-survey-reveals-structured-scenario-planning-separates-top-performing-corporate-finance-teams) , fielded with 332 corporate finance practitioners, found that only 43% of organizations use rolling forecasts at all, and that teams using structured scenario planning scored 14% higher on strategic alignment. So ask to see a redacted forward-looking work product. A rolling cash forecast with its assumptions labeled, a scenario comparison, a one-decision model. Not a historical profit and loss statement with a variance column.[Cash flow forecasting for growing businesses](https://www.indinero.com/blog/cash-flow-forecasting-for-growing-businesses/) covers what that artifact should actually contain.


**3. Who does the work, and what happens when that person changes.** Proposals describe services. Engagements get delivered by people.


Ask who, not what.


Get these in writing. The named individual doing the analytical work, and their background rather than the firm’s. Whether that person sits in your meetings, or whether a senior person sells and a junior person delivers. How many other businesses they carry at once. What happens if they leave or get reassigned, including who the named backup is and what’s documented. Whether your models and reporting templates stay yours at the end. A solo practitioner and a firm-delivered engagement genuinely differ here, and neither is automatically better. One mind gives you continuity and no handoff risk, until the day the handoff risk is total. A firm gives you bench depth, and your job is to verify the named person is senior enough to do the thinking. Either structure works. An unanswered continuity question doesn’t.


**4. Cadence and responsiveness.** Fractional means scoped time, not reduced seniority. “A few days a month” covers a wide range of realities, so find out what you’re buying. Pin down the standing meeting rhythm and what happens inside each one. Pin down who attends, because a CFO who never meets operations will never fix operational margin. Pin down what arrives before the meeting versus during it, since a package circulated two days ahead with a written point of view is a different service from a screen-share walkthrough. Then pin down response time for an unscheduled question, in hours or business days, and how urgent work gets in when a lender asks for something or a large customer goes slow on payment. Length isn’t quality. A candidate who answers a reporting complaint by proposing more pages is solving the wrong problem.


**5. Coordination with the people who keep the books.** A CFO designs the reporting roadmap and uses the numbers. A CFO does not produce them. If a candidate’s plan for fixing your reporting is to do your bookkeeping, you’re paying for strategic leadership and receiving accounting work.


Role Owns


Bookkeeper Recording transactions, reconciliations, payables and receivables processing, payroll input


Controller Accurate and timely closed books, internal controls, the close calendar, the integrity of the reporting package


CFO Forecasting, profitability and margin analysis, decision modeling, capital allocation, pricing, and the design of the finance function over time


So ask who owns the chart of accounts and who approves changes to it. A CFO should specify what the chart needs to reveal. Accounting should implement and maintain it. Ask who owns the close calendar, what the CFO needs from accounting and by which day of the month, and what happens when a number lands late or wrong. If your bookkeeping sits with an outside provider, ask how the CFO will work with them and whether they’ve done it before. The lines between these three roles are worth understanding before you interview anyone, and[controller vs comptroller vs CFO](https://www.indinero.com/blog/controller-vs-comptroller-vs-cfo/) draws them plainly.


### What the scope of work should spell out


A fractional CFO scope of work should be specific enough that an outside reader could tell, from the document alone, what gets delivered, by whom, how often, and what’s excluded. If it reads like a service brochure, it isn’t a scope of work.


Professional standards set the floor here, which is your leverage. Under the AICPA’s[Statement on Standards for Consulting Services No. 1](https://egrove.olemiss.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1311&context=aicpa_prof) , codified as CS section 100, a practitioner has to establish an understanding with the client about each party’s responsibilities and about the nature, scope, and limitations of the services. Vagueness isn’t an industry norm. It’s a choice. Writing in the Journal of Accountancy, Sarah Beckett Ference, CPA, advises that an advisory[engagement letter be detailed and specific about what you are going to do for the client and how often](https://www.journalofaccountancy.com/issues/2026/apr/tips-for-writing-cas-engagement-letters/) , that it list the actual deliverables, and that scope changes get captured in a signed amendment or a change log rather than absorbed informally. A CFO advises and models. The owner decides.


- **Objective.** The problem the engagement exists to solve, and what’s true at 90 days and at 12 months that isn’t true now.
- **Named deliverables.** The recurring outputs, such as a rolling 13-week cash forecast and a monthly leadership package with written commentary. Then the one-time ones, such as a margin analysis by segment.
- **Cadence and calendar.** Meetings and attendees, a delivery date for each output stated as a day of the month, and a defined response time for unscheduled questions.
- **People.** The named individual, anyone else who touches the work, and the documented backup.
- **Responsibilities on both sides.** What the provider does, and what your team supplies and by when. Closed books by a stated day.
- **The boundary with accounting and tax.** What the CFO doesn’t do, who produces the numbers, and how a late close gets escalated. Tax planning coordination can be in scope while return preparation sits with the tax team.
- **Explicit exclusions.** A written out-of-scope list. This one clause prevents most disputes.
- **Term, review, and exit.** Term length, a 90-day checkpoint, notice period for either side, and what you keep on the way out.
- **Fee structure as a structure.** Retainer versus project, what the retainer includes, and how out-of-scope work gets handled. Agree the mechanics before the number.


## The Questions That Reveal Whether the Fit Is Real


Good diagnostic questions share one property. A polished generalist can’t answer them without revealing whether they’ve done the work. The questions to ask a fractional CFO are about mechanism, sequence, and a specific past situation, never about philosophy. Ask for a philosophy and you’ll get a thoughtful answer from someone who has never run a collections cycle.


**On operating depth**


- “Walk me through a business with complexity close to ours. What was broken when you arrived, what did you change first, and what moved.” A strong answer is a sequence with named mechanics and a measured result over a stated period. A weak one sounds like “I helped them get visibility into their numbers.”
- “Which of these have you personally handled: multi-entity consolidation, inventory turns, multi-state payroll, covenant reporting, progress billing.” Make them answer line by line.
- “Tell me about a recommendation you made that didn’t work. What did you miss.”


**On forward-looking work**


- “What’s the difference between a rolling forecast and modeling a single decision, and when do you use each.”
- “How often does your forecast get updated, and what triggers an update between scheduled cycles.”
- “If I asked you today which of our products or customer segments is least profitable, what would you need to answer that, and how long would it take.”


**On who does the work and how fast**


- “Who exactly will do our analytical work, what’s their background, and will they be in our meetings.”
- “How many other businesses does that person support right now, and what happens in week one if they become unavailable.”
- “Describe the first 90 days week by week. What exists at day 90 that doesn’t exist today.”
- “What’s your response time for an unscheduled question, in hours or business days.”


**On the boundary with accounting**


- “Who owns our chart of accounts, and who approves changes to it.”
- “What do you need from our bookkeeper or controller, and by which day of the month.”
- “Where does your work stop and our accounting work start. Say it in one sentence.”


**On scope honesty**


- “What is explicitly not in scope.”
- “What would you tell me to fix before engaging a CFO at all.” A strong answer names a books, close, or systems problem and tells you to fix it first. A weak answer is always yes.
- “What kind of business are you a bad fit for.”


Then the references, which most owners handle too gently. Ask for two at comparable complexity, and ask each of them one question. What decision did you make differently because of this engagement. A reference who can only say the reporting improved is describing a controller, not a CFO. For a plain-language map of the work itself, see[what CFO services cover](https://www.indinero.com/faq/what-are-cfo-services/) .


## When a Fractional CFO Is Not What Your Business Needs


Three problems get mistaken for a CFO problem, and a CFO engagement won’t fix any of them. Books that aren’t accurate. A close that takes too long. A tax question. Name the real problem first, because strategic leadership layered on unreliable inputs produces confident decisions built on wrong numbers.


**“Our numbers aren’t reliable.”** You don’t trust the monthly profit and loss statement. Reconciliations lag. Revenue lands in the wrong period. Nobody can produce margin by product or customer, because the chart of accounts was never built to show it. Two reports give two answers. That’s an accounting problem wearing a CFO costume. A CFO can specify what the chart of accounts needs to reveal, but the fix itself is accounting work and it comes first. Start with[indinero accounting services](https://www.indinero.com/services/accounting-services/) , or with[online bookkeeping services](https://www.indinero.com/services/online-bookkeeping-services/) if the gap sits at the transaction level.


**“Our close takes too long.”** The month-end package arrives three weeks after month end, so every decision gets made on quarter-old information. No close calendar exists. The same reconciliations get rediscovered every month. There’s a benchmark you can measure yourself against. APQC’s research on monthly close cycle time, covering 2,300 organizations, puts the median at 6.4 calendar days from running the trial balance to completed financial statements, with the top quartile at 4.8 days or less and the bottom quartile at 10 days or more ([Metric of the Month: Cycle Time for Monthly Close](https://www.cfo.com/news/metric-of-the-month-cycle-time-for-monthly-close/659297/) ). The same work names data quality as the dominant barrier and a standardized chart of accounts as worth roughly two days on its own. If your close runs well past 10 days, close discipline is the first investment, not strategic leadership. A CFO advises on the roadmap. Accounting executes it.


**“We have a tax question.”** Multi-state filing exposure, an entity structure question, a return deadline, a notice from a tax authority, or a planning question tied to one transaction. A CFO coordinates on tax planning as part of capital allocation and decision modeling, and does not prepare or file returns. That work belongs with[business tax services](https://www.indinero.com/services/business-tax-services/) .


**“We need accurate reporting on a reliable schedule.”** That’s controller work. Stewardship, accuracy, timeliness, control. Plenty of businesses need a controller now and a CFO in a year, and saying so is more useful than selling you the wrong layer.


A fractional CFO genuinely is the right call when the books are reliable, the close is predictable, and the open questions are forward-looking. Where is cash going over the next 13 weeks and why. Which segments actually make money. Should we sign this contract at this price. Buy or lease. Those are strategic questions sitting on sound inputs, which is the condition under which financial leadership earns its keep.


## How Indinero Approaches CFO Engagements


Indinero’s CFO Services bring forward-looking financial leadership to owners and leadership teams of established, growing businesses, delivered fractionally and coordinated with the teams that keep the books. Read everything above as criteria. Read this section as our answers to them.


The work sits under four themes.


- **See Clearly.** Profitability and margin analysis broken out by product, service, customer, and segment, with the real unit economics underneath it. A tight metric set built around the few indicators that move your business. Management reporting written as a forward-looking narrative instead of a historical recap.
- **Plan Forward.** Continuous by design. Rolling forecasts of revenue, expenses, profitability, and cash impact, updated as conditions change. Cash flow and working capital management aimed at cash flow predictability. Scenario planning that stress-tests hiring, expansion, and capital investment before anything is committed.
- **Decide Well.** Event-driven, one decision at a time. Lease versus buy, the true margin on a major contract, a new territory, an executive hire. Capital allocation and CapEx strategy with return modeling behind each option. Pricing grounded in real cost data. Interim CFO leadership when a finance leadership gap opens.
- **Build Value.** Process improvement across close, billing and collections, and spend. Working Capital Optimization aimed at days sales outstanding, inventory drag, and vendor terms. Finance function design, including the boundaries between bookkeeping, controller oversight, and CFO leadership.


Here’s the criterion we answer structurally rather than with a promise. The boundary question in dimension five is the one most engagements leave open, because the CFO and the bookkeeper usually work for two different companies. Bookkeeping, accounting, tax, and CFO work all sit inside indinero, so the close calendar can be built around the forecast cycle, definitions get shared instead of negotiated, and nobody has to assign blame when a number lands late. The CFO role stays distinct and strategic. It uses the numbers. It does not produce them.


Continuity is the other criterion worth answering plainly rather than reassuringly. Continuous operations since 2009, 500+ regular customers, and 100+ years combined team experience mean that “what happens if the person assigned to us changes” has a documented answer behind it. Engagements get scoped to the complexity in front of them, not sold as fixed packages. And if the honest answer for your business turns out to be accurate books, a faster close, or a filing question, that’s still work we do. Different team, same side of the table.


Choosing a fractional CFO isn’t really a procurement exercise. It’s a judgment about whether one person can carry the forward-looking questions your business has outgrown, verified before you sign rather than discovered in month four. If you’re running that evaluation now, reach out for a free consultation with our[CFO Services](https://www.indinero.com/services/cfo-services/) team. We’d like to hear what your business is working on.


## Frequently asked questions


These are the questions owners and leadership teams bring us while they’re still comparing candidates. If yours isn’t below, it’s worth a conversation.


### What should an owner look for in a fractional CFO?


Owners should look for operating depth at comparable complexity, forward-looking work, a named person doing the analysis, defined cadence, and a clear accounting boundary. Testing four of the five and hoping on the fifth isn’t a pass. The highest-yield test is whether a candidate separates continuous rolling forecasts from modeling one discrete decision, since blurring the two usually means reporting carrying a strategic label. Owners come to indinero holding proposals that all read as qualified, so the criteria matter more than the credentials.


### How much industry experience does a fractional CFO actually need?


A fractional CFO needs experience with your operational complexity more than your industry label, and complexity adjacency usually predicts fit better. Someone who has run multi-entity consolidation, inventory turns, multi-state payroll, and covenant reporting in another industry typically fits better than a same-industry candidate who never handled any of it. Indinero scopes CFO engagements to the complexity a business actually has, not to a sector it happens to sit in. Ask line by line which mechanics a candidate has personally run.


### How do you check a fractional CFO’s track record before signing?


Check a fractional CFO’s track record with two references at comparable operational complexity, asking each what decision they made differently because of the engagement. A reference who can only say the reporting improved is describing a controller, not a CFO. Then ask the candidate to walk through a business close to yours, naming what was broken, what changed first, and what moved. Request a redacted forward-looking work product too, such as a rolling cash forecast with labeled assumptions.


### What should the engagement spell out in writing?


The engagement should name deliverables, cadence, the individual doing the work, responsibilities on both sides, explicit exclusions, and the boundary with accounting and tax. The AICPA’s Statement on Standards for Consulting Services No. 1, codified as CS section 100, requires a practitioner to establish an understanding with the client on each party’s responsibilities and on the nature, scope, and limitations of the services. Indinero spells out the accounting boundary, since the CFO uses the numbers rather than producing them.


### How long does it take to know whether the engagement is working?


Ninety days is the honest checkpoint for a fractional CFO engagement, and the scope should state what exists at day 90 that doesn’t today. Sooner than that, watch for a forecast that gets updated when conditions move, a margin question answered in days instead of weeks, and a decision you made with numbers behind it. Structural change in cash flow predictability and margin takes closer to a year. Indinero writes that 90-day checkpoint into the scope rather than leaving it to month four.


### What happens if the person assigned to your account changes?


If your assigned lead changes, what happens depends on what you settled in writing: the named backup, the documented models, and a defined handoff. A solo practitioner carries no handoff risk until the day that risk is total. A firm gives you bench depth, and your job is verifying the named person is senior enough to do the thinking. Indinero has maintained continuous operations since 2009 with 500+ regular customers, so a staffing change has a process behind it rather than an improvised answer.
